findings.title: Every valid order line panics
findings.detail: The note loop indexes fields[len(fields)] on every record with at least two fields, so even a valid order line panics when loaded. Remove the loop because the parsed line does not use the note.

findings.title: Order reservations bypass stock limits
findings.detail: ReserveLines updates Reserved directly and returns success for quantities that exceed available stock. A negative quantity also reduces existing reservations, and zero is silently skipped. Apply the same positive-count and capacity checks as Stock.Reserve before changing stock.

findings.title: Concurrent reservations can lose updates
findings.detail: ReserveLines writes Reserved without taking the mutex used by Reserve and Free. Concurrent reservations against the same stock can lose updates even when both calls report success. Perform reservation checks and updates under the same stock mutex.

findings.title: A failed order leaves earlier lines reserved
findings.detail: If a later line names an unknown item, earlier lines have already changed stock, but the error gives callers no account of those changes. Retrying after correcting the item reserves those lines again. Validate the full order before applying any stock changes, including the combined quantities of repeated items.

findings.title: Invalid quantities are silently accepted
findings.detail: Once the parser panic is fixed, ignoring the Atoi error lets a typo such as `widget;two` become a zero quantity that ReserveLines silently skips. Return the conversion error so LoadOrder rejects the malformed order.

findings.title: Order files are never closed
findings.detail: LoadOrder leaves the file open on every path after os.Open succeeds. Repeated loads can exhaust file descriptors before garbage collection reclaims them. Defer file.Close immediately after checking the open error.

findings.title: Parsing any valid order line panics
findings.detail: The note loop accesses fields[len(fields)] for every input with at least two fields. A valid line such as "widget;2" panics immediately, and loading a file containing that line panics too.

findings.title: Invalid quantities pass parsing without an error
findings.detail: ParseLine discards the error from strconv.Atoi. Once the preceding loop panic is fixed, malformed quantities can be returned as zero and out-of-range quantities as an integer limit, both with a nil error.

findings.title: Loading orders leaks file descriptors
findings.detail: After os.Open succeeds, LoadOrder never closes the file. Repeated calls can accumulate open descriptors until the runtime finalizes the files, exhausting the process's descriptor limit.

findings.title: The loader rejects valid orders with long notes
findings.detail: The default Scanner buffer imposes a roughly 64 KiB line limit. A file whose first line has a valid item and quantity followed by a longer optional note fails with a scanner error before parsing. The order format specifies no such limit.

findings.title: Batch reservations can exceed stock capacity
findings.detail: ReserveLines increments Reserved without checking free stock. An order that exceeds available units returns success and leaves Reserved above Capacity. A sufficiently large addition can also wrap the counter.

findings.title: Batch reservations accept zero and negative quantities
findings.detail: Reserve rejects counts below one. ReserveLines silently skips zero and adds negative quantities to Reserved, so an invalid order can release previously reserved units or make Reserved negative while returning success.

findings.title: Batch reservations race on shared stock
findings.detail: ReserveLines updates Reserved without taking the stock mutex. It races with Reserve, Free, and other calls to ReserveLines on the same stock. Concurrent increments can lose reservations.

findings.title: An unknown item leaves earlier reservations applied
findings.detail: When a later item is unknown, ReserveLines returns an error after changing stock for earlier lines. The return value provides no record of which lines were applied, and retrying the whole order after fixing the unknown item reserves those earlier quantities again.

findings.title: A nil stock entry crashes batch reservation
findings.detail: A key mapped to a nil *Stock passes the presence check. A line with that key and a nonzero quantity then dereferences the nil pointer and panics.

findings.title: ParseLine panics with index out of range on every valid line
findings.detail: The note loop runs `for index := 2; index <= len(fields); index++` and reads fields[index]. When index == len(fields), that read is out of bounds. For the minimal valid input "item;3", len(fields) == 2, so the loop reads fields[2] and panics right away. Every line LoadOrder reads with at least two fields crashes the program. The fix is to use `index < len(fields)`, or to drop the unused note code entirely, since its value is thrown away (`_ = note`).

findings.title: ReserveLines skips the capacity check, the positive-count check and the lock
findings.detail: ReserveLines runs `stock.Reserved += line.Quantity` directly. Reserve exists to enforce Reserved+count <= Capacity, to reject counts that are not positive, and to hold the mutex. Bypassing it lets orders overbook stock with no error, lets negative quantities lower Reserved, and races with concurrent Reserve and Free calls. The fix is to call `stock.Reserve(line.Quantity)` and return its error. Zero and negative quantities should then be rejected, not skipped.

findings.title: Bad quantity is silently treated as 0
findings.detail: ParseLine discards the error from strconv.Atoi (`quantity, _ :=`). A typo such as "item;3x" or "item;" therefore parses as Quantity 0, and ReserveLines then skips it with `continue`. The order line disappears without any error. The fix is to return an error when Atoi fails, and to reject quantities of 0 or less.

findings.title: A failed order leaves its earlier lines reserved
findings.detail: When a later line hits an unknown item (or, once F2 is fixed, ErrNotEnough), ReserveLines returns an error, but the reservations for the lines before it stay in place. The order is rejected while part of its stock remains reserved. The fix is to validate every line before reserving anything, or to undo the earlier reservations when a line fails.

findings.title: Order file is never closed
findings.detail: LoadOrder opens the file with os.Open but never closes it, so each call leaks a file descriptor. The fix is to add `defer file.Close()` right after the error check.

findings.title: Note loop indexes past the end of fields and panics on every line
findings.detail: The loop runs `for index := 2; index <= len(fields); index++` and reads fields[index]. Once index reaches len(fields), the read is out of range. With the minimal valid input "item;3", len(fields)==2, so fields[2] is read right away and the code panics. Every line therefore crashes ParseLine, and through it LoadOrder. The condition should be `index < len(fields)`.

findings.title: ReserveLines changes Reserved without taking the stock mutex
findings.detail: `stock.Reserved += line.Quantity` runs without stock.mutex. Reserve and Free hold that lock, so concurrent use is a data race. Updates can be lost and Free can read a torn value. It should call stock.Reserve(line.Quantity), which takes the lock.

findings.title: ReserveLines skips the capacity check and overbooks stock
findings.detail: Reserve rejects a reservation when Reserved+count > Capacity, but ReserveLines adds the quantity with no check. An order bigger than the free stock succeeds and pushes Reserved above Capacity, so Free goes negative. ErrNotEnough is never returned.

findings.title: Bad quantity is silently treated as 0 and the line is skipped
findings.detail: The error from strconv.Atoi is thrown away. A malformed quantity such as "abc" or "3x" becomes 0 and ParseLine returns no error. ReserveLines then skips any line with Quantity == 0. A corrupt order line is dropped without any error, so the order is quietly under-reserved.

findings.title: Negative quantities are accepted and lower Reserved
findings.detail: ParseLine accepts negative numbers, and ReserveLines skips only Quantity == 0. A line like "widget;-5" is applied as Reserved += -5. That releases units other orders hold and can push Reserved below zero, so Free reports more stock than Capacity. Reserve rejects count <= 0, but this path does not.

findings.title: LoadOrder never closes the opened file
findings.detail: os.Open is called with no defer file.Close(). Every call leaks a file descriptor, including the early return on a parse error. A long-running process that loads many orders will run out of descriptors.

findings.title: ReserveLines leaves earlier lines reserved when a later line fails
findings.detail: When a line names an unknown item, ReserveLines returns an error, but the earlier lines' reservations stay applied and are not rolled back. The caller sees the order as failed while stock stays held for part of it. The function should validate all lines first or roll back on error.

findings.title: Cache misses fresh entries and serves expired values
findings.detail: At line 39, Get returns a miss when the expiration is in the future, then returns the stored value at and after expiration. This defeats caching while entries are fresh and silently serves stale lookup results afterward. Return a miss when !found.expires.After(cache.Now()).

findings.title: Concurrent cache reads and writes can terminate the process
findings.detail: At line 35, Get reads the same map that Put writes under cache.mutex. A lookup that overlaps a write, even for a different key, can terminate the process with a concurrent map read and write error. Acquire cache.mutex around the map read in Get.

findings.title: Unchecked releases can lead to overselling
findings.detail: At line 51, Release subtracts count without checking it. A duplicate cancellation or a release for too many units can drive Reserved below zero, making Free report more than Capacity and allowing later reservations to oversell. A negative count can also increase Reserved. Under the existing lock, reject nonpositive counts and counts greater than Reserved before changing stock.

findings.title: Cache rejects fresh entries and serves expired values
findings.detail: Get returns a miss when the expiration time is still in the future. At the expiration time and afterward, it returns the stale value until that key is overwritten.

findings.title: Concurrent cache reads and writes can crash the process
findings.detail: Get reads entries without acquiring the mutex used by Put. A read that overlaps a write races even when the operations use different keys, and Go can terminate the process with a concurrent map read and map write error.

findings.title: Expired cache entries accumulate without bound
findings.detail: Put adds keys to the map and no code removes them. A long-lived cache that sees a steady stream of distinct keys retains every key after expiration, so memory use can grow until the process runs out of memory.

findings.title: Invalid release counts corrupt the reserved total
findings.detail: Releasing more units than are reserved makes Reserved negative, causing Free to report more than Capacity and allowing subsequent reservations to oversell. A negative release count increases Reserved and can push it above Capacity.

findings.title: Release races with order-line reservations
findings.detail: Release holds the stock mutex, but ReserveLines updates the same Reserved field without acquiring it. Calling the two methods concurrently on the same stock can lose either update even when both counts are valid.

findings.title: Expiry check is inverted: fresh entries miss, expired entries hit
findings.detail: Get returns a miss when `found.expires.After(cache.Now())`, i.e. while the entry is still valid, and returns the value only after it has expired. So the cache never serves fresh values and always serves stale ones from then on, with no error. Callers will act on outdated stock figures. Fix: return a miss when `!found.expires.After(cache.Now())` (it has expired), and return the value otherwise.

findings.title: Get reads the map without holding the mutex
findings.detail: Put writes `cache.entries` while holding `cache.mutex`, but Get reads the map with no lock. If Get and Put run at the same time, that is a data race on a Go map. The runtime can stop the program with "concurrent map read and map write". Fix: call `cache.mutex.Lock(); defer cache.mutex.Unlock()` at the start of Get.

findings.title: Release does not check count, so Reserved can go negative and Free can exceed Capacity
findings.detail: Release subtracts any count without checking it. A double release, a release larger than what is reserved, or a negative count leaves Reserved negative or too high. A negative Reserved makes Free() larger than Capacity, so later Reserve calls can oversell, and nothing reports the error. Reserve already rejects count <= 0. Fix: reject count <= 0 and count > stock.Reserved, and return an error (as Reserve does) instead of changing Reserved.

findings.title: Expiry check inverted: live entries are misses, expired entries are returned
findings.detail: Get returns a miss when found.expires.After(Now()), which is exactly when the entry is still valid, and returns the value once it has expired. The cache never serves a fresh value and always serves stale ones.

findings.title: Get reads the map without taking the mutex
findings.detail: Put locks cache.mutex before writing entries, but Get reads cache.entries without locking. A Get that runs at the same time as a Put is a data race on a Go map, and the runtime can abort the process with 'concurrent map read and map write'.

findings.title: Release does not validate count, so Reserved can go negative
findings.detail: Release subtracts count with no check that count is positive or no larger than Reserved. Releasing too much, or releasing twice, makes Reserved negative. Free() then reports more than Capacity, and later Reserve calls can oversell the stock. A negative count silently increases Reserved instead.

findings.title: Expired entries are never evicted
findings.detail: Nothing ever deletes an entry from entries, including after it expires. With many distinct keys, the map grows without bound, which leaks memory.

findings.title: Retry reports success after all attempts fail
findings.detail: After every attempt fails, Retry returns nil and discards the last error. A caller can proceed as though a reservation or write succeeded when it never did. Return the last error after the loop.

findings.title: A failed export can erase existing data
findings.detail: The shell opens and truncates the report before grep validates the pattern or reads the stock file. A mistyped stock path or invalid pattern can erase the previous report. If both paths refer to the same file, the stock data itself is erased. Reject a destination that aliases the stock file and replace the report from a temporary file only after a successful export.

findings.title: Pagination silently drops the last partial page
findings.detail: Page returns nil whenever fewer than size items remain. With 11 items and a page size of 10, page 1 looks empty and the eleventh item disappears from ordinary pagination. Return nil when the start is outside the slice and clamp the end to the slice length.

findings.title: Export lets the shell interpret filenames and patterns
findings.detail: Export interpolates all three inputs into shell source. Ordinary path characters can change which files the command reads or writes, and shell syntax in an input can execute commands with the caller's permissions. Open the stock and output files in Go, connect them to grep's stdin and stdout, and pass the pattern as a separate argument with -e.

findings.title: Export reports an empty result as an error
findings.detail: Grep returns status 1 when a valid filter matches no lines. Export propagates it as a failure even though an empty report is the correct result. Treat status 1 as a successful empty export and preserve other execution errors.

findings.title: Large pagination inputs can panic
findings.detail: Large positive page numbers or sizes can overflow the multiplication or addition. The bounds check can then accept invalid indices and the slice operation can panic. Check that the page starts within the input using division before multiplying, then compute the end from the number of items remaining.

findings.title: Retry waits after the last attempt
findings.detail: Retry sleeps after the final failed call even though there is no next attempt. Sleep only if another attempt remains.

findings.title: Export lets caller-controlled input become shell syntax
findings.detail: Export interpolates the pattern and both paths into a command interpreted by `sh`. Shell syntax in any of those inputs can execute commands with the process's privileges. Ordinary inputs such as an apostrophe in a pattern or a space in a path can also break the export. Invoke `grep` directly with separate arguments and handle report output in Go.

findings.title: Grep can misinterpret patterns and filenames as options
findings.detail: Shell quoting ends before `grep` parses its arguments. A pattern or stock-file path beginning with a dash can be interpreted as an option, and a stock-file argument of `-` reads standard input. Pass the pattern with `-e`, end option parsing before the file operand, and ensure a file named `-` is addressed as a path.

findings.title: Export can truncate the source inventory
findings.detail: The shell truncates the report before grep opens the stock file. If both paths refer to the same file, including through a link, Export erases the source inventory before reading it.

findings.title: Export reports zero matches as a failure
findings.detail: Grep exits with status 1 when it finds zero matches. Export propagates that status as an error even though it successfully produces the expected empty report, so callers cannot treat an empty result as success.

findings.title: Page drops the final partially filled page
findings.detail: Page returns nil whenever the requested end exceeds the item count, even when the start is in range. For example, page 1 with five items and a page size of three drops the final two items. Clamp the end to the item count for a page that starts in range.

findings.title: Page index arithmetic can overflow and panic
findings.detail: Both the offset multiplication and the end calculation can overflow `int` for positive inputs. The upper-bound check can accept a wrapped result, causing an out-of-range request to return the wrong items or panic during slicing. Validate the page number before multiplying and bound the slice length before adding.

findings.title: Retry returns success after exhausting all attempts
findings.detail: When every attempt fails, Retry discards the last error and returns nil. Callers can then proceed on the assumption that an operation succeeded even though every invocation failed.

findings.title: Retry waits after the final failed attempt
findings.detail: Retry sleeps after the final failed attempt even though no further call is scheduled. With one attempt, a failure incurs the full pause despite there being no retry.

findings.title: Retry reports success when every attempt failed
findings.detail: After the loop the function returns `nil` instead of `last`. When all attempts fail, the caller receives nil and continues as if the work had succeeded, so the failure goes unnoticed. This also contradicts the doc comment, which says the last error is returned. Fix: `return last`. A smaller related issue: the loop also sleeps after the final failed attempt, which wastes one pause. Skip the sleep when attempt == attempts-1.

findings.title: Export builds a shell command from unquoted input (command injection)
findings.detail: `sh -c "grep '"+pattern+"' "+stockFile+" > "+report` inserts pattern, stockFile and report straight into a shell string. A pattern that contains a single quote (for example an item name such as O'Brien), or a path that contains a space, makes the command fail or behave differently. Crafted input can run any command. The `>` redirect also creates or overwrites whatever path the report argument resolves to. Fix: do not use the shell. Run `exec.Command("grep", "-e", pattern, "--", stockFile)`, set cmd.Stdout to a file opened with os.Create(report), and handle grep's exit status 1 (no match) on purpose. Better still, do the filtering in Go.

findings.title: Page drops the final partial page
findings.detail: When `end > len(items)` the function returns nil. A final page holding fewer than `size` items is never returned. For example, 25 items with size 10 give pages 0 and 1, and page 2 (items 20–24) is empty, so those items silently disappear from paged listings. Fix: return nil only when `start >= len(items)`, otherwise cap `end` at len(items). Also consider guarding `number*size` against overflow.

findings.title: Shell command injection through pattern, stockFile and report
findings.detail: Export builds a command string by joining pattern, stockFile and report and runs it with `sh -c`. A pattern that contains a single quote, such as `x' /etc/passwd; rm -rf ~ #`, ends the quoting and runs any command the caller chooses. File names that contain spaces or shell metacharacters (`;`, `$()`, `>`) are also interpreted by the shell. The fix is to call exec.Command("grep", "--", pattern, stockFile) directly and write its output to a file opened with os.Create.

findings.title: Retry returns nil when every attempt failed
findings.detail: When all the attempts fail, the loop exits and the function returns nil instead of `last`. Callers treat a failed operation as a success. The doc comment promises the last error, so this result is wrong.

findings.title: Last partial page is dropped (returns nil)
findings.detail: When end > len(items), Page returns nil instead of clamping end to len(items). The final page is lost whenever it holds fewer than size items. For example, with 5 items and size 2, page 2 returns nil instead of [item4]. A list shorter than size returns nil for page 0. The fix is to return nil only when start >= len(items) and otherwise set end = min(end, len(items)).

findings.title: Sleeps needlessly after the final failed attempt
findings.detail: time.Sleep(pause) also runs after the last attempt, so a call that fails completely is delayed by an extra pause for nothing.

findings.title: No matching items is reported as an error
findings.detail: grep exits with status 1 when no line matches, so Export returns an error for an export that is valid but empty. The caller cannot tell this case apart from a real failure, such as a missing stock file, which gives exit status 2.

findings.title: Every structurally valid order line panics
findings.detail: The loop allows index == len(fields), then reads fields[index]. Every line with at least two fields panics, with or without a note. LoadOrder propagates the panic when it encounters such a line.

findings.title: Order reservations can exceed stock capacity
findings.detail: The direct update ignores the stock's remaining capacity. Reserving 6 units from a stock with 5 free succeeds and leaves Free() at -1. Multiple lines for the same item can also exceed capacity cumulatively.

findings.title: Order reservations race with other stock operations
findings.detail: The update reads and writes Reserved outside the mutex used by Reserve and Free. Concurrent reservations can overwrite each other, and concurrent calls to Free race with the write.

findings.title: Order reservations accept nonpositive quantities
findings.detail: A negative quantity reduces Reserved and makes previously reserved units appear available. A zero quantity silently succeeds. Stock.Reserve rejects both values.

findings.title: Quantity conversion failures are silently accepted
findings.detail: The discarded Atoi error lets invalid numeric text become zero and out-of-range integers become clamped values while ParseLine reports success. The loop panic currently prevents execution from reaching this conversion.

findings.title: Loading orders leaks file descriptors
findings.detail: After a successful os.Open, the function never closes the file. Even empty files and files rejected with a parse error leave descriptors open until garbage collection, so repeated calls can exhaust the process's descriptor limit.

findings.title: An unknown item leaves earlier reservations applied
findings.detail: If a later item is missing from the map, the function returns an error after committing earlier reservations. The result does not identify which lines were applied, so retrying the order after adding the missing item reserves the earlier lines again.

findings.title: A nil stock entry crashes order reservation
findings.detail: A map entry with a nil *Stock passes the presence check. A nonzero quantity for that item then dereferences the nil pointer and panics.

findings.title: The scanner rejects valid orders with long notes
findings.detail: The default Scanner token limit rejects lines with long notes before ParseLine sees them. A line over 64 KiB can follow the documented format and still cause LoadOrder to return a scanner error.

findings.title: Note loop indexes past the end of fields and panics on every line
findings.detail: The loop is `for index := 2; index <= len(fields); index++ { note += fields[index] }`. On its last pass `index == len(fields)`, so `fields[index]` panics with index out of range. This happens for every valid line: with "a;3", index 2 equals len 2. As a result, `LoadOrder` crashes the process on any non-empty order file. Fix: use `index < len(fields)`, or drop the unused note code entirely. It is discarded with `_ = note` anyway.

findings.title: ReserveLines skips the capacity check and the mutex
findings.detail: `ReserveLines` does `stock.Reserved += line.Quantity` directly. It never checks capacity, so an order larger than the free stock is fully reserved and no error is returned (`Free()` can go negative). It also skips `stock.mutex`, so it races with `Reserve` and `Free`. A negative quantity, which `ParseLine` accepts, lowers `Reserved` and frees stock that other orders hold. Fix: call `stock.Reserve(line.Quantity)` for each line and return its error. This also rejects quantities of 0 or less.

findings.title: A quantity that fails to parse silently becomes 0 and the line is dropped
findings.detail: `quantity, _ := strconv.Atoi(...)` throws away the parse error. A typo such as "widget;1O" or "widget;" yields Quantity 0. `ReserveLines` then skips that line with `continue`, so the order is accepted as successful with the line missing. Fix: return the Atoi error with the line text, and reject quantities of 0 or less in `ParseLine`.

findings.title: An unknown item partway through leaves the order half-reserved
findings.detail: Lines before the unknown item are already added to `Reserved` when the error is returned, and nothing rolls them back. The caller sees a failed order, but stock stays reserved for it. Fix: check every item exists (and, after F2, that every line fits) before changing anything, or undo the earlier reservations on error.

findings.title: The order file is never closed
findings.detail: `os.Open` is never paired with `Close`, so each call leaks a file descriptor. Fix: add `defer file.Close()` right after the error check.

findings.title: ParseLine indexes one past the end of fields and panics on every line
findings.detail: The note loop runs `for index := 2; index <= len(fields); index++` and reads fields[index]. When index == len(fields), that read is out of range. A plain "item;3" line has len(fields)==2, so it panics on fields[2] right away. Every valid line therefore crashes ParseLine and LoadOrder. The condition should be `index < len(fields)`.

findings.title: ReserveLines changes Reserved without taking the stock mutex
findings.detail: `stock.Reserved += line.Quantity` writes the shared field without stock.mutex. Reserve and Free take that lock, so a concurrent call to either races with this write. Updates can be lost and Free can read torn or stale values.

findings.title: ReserveLines skips the capacity and sign checks and overbooks stock
findings.detail: ReserveLines adds the quantity straight to Reserved instead of calling Reserve. It never checks Reserved+count against Capacity, so an order can reserve more than exists and Free goes negative. It also accepts negative quantities, which lower Reserved and release stock that was never reserved by this order.

findings.title: ReserveLines leaves earlier lines reserved when a later line fails
findings.detail: Lines are applied one at a time. If a later line names an unknown item, the function returns an error but keeps the reservations already made for earlier lines. Nothing rolls them back, so a failed order still holds stock and the caller cannot tell how much.

findings.title: Bad quantity is read as 0 and the line is silently skipped
findings.detail: The error from strconv.Atoi is thrown away, so a quantity such as "abc" or "" becomes 0 with no error. ReserveLines then skips lines with quantity 0 (`continue`). A malformed line is dropped quietly instead of being rejected, and the order is fulfilled short.

findings.title: LoadOrder never closes the file it opens
findings.detail: os.Open is called with no matching `defer file.Close()`. The descriptor leaks on every call, on both the success and the error paths. A long-running process that loads many orders will run out of file descriptors.

findings.title: Lines longer than the scanner buffer fail LoadOrder
findings.detail: bufio.Scanner keeps its default 64KB token limit. A line longer than that stops the scan, and LoadOrder returns bufio.ErrTooLong after reading only part of the file.

findings.title: Valid order lines panic during parsing
findings.detail: The note loop runs with index equal to len(fields), so every line with at least two fields panics. A normal order file containing a line such as widget;2 therefore panics in LoadOrder. Remove the unused note loop.

findings.title: Orders can corrupt reservation totals
findings.detail: ReserveLines adds directly to Reserved, bypassing the capacity and positive-count checks in Stock.Reserve. An order can exceed available stock or reduce an existing reservation with a negative quantity, and the call still succeeds. Apply the same quantity and capacity checks before updating stock and return ErrNotEnough when demand exceeds available units.

findings.title: Concurrent reservations can lose updates
findings.detail: ReserveLines writes Reserved without acquiring the mutex used by Stock.Reserve and Stock.Free. Concurrent reservations can overwrite each other's increments, and concurrent availability reads race with the write. Use the same stock mutex for every reservation check and update.

findings.title: A failed order leaves partial reservations
findings.detail: If a later line names an unknown item, ReserveLines returns an error after reserving the earlier lines. The error gives callers no indication of which reservations were applied, so correcting the item and retrying the order can reserve the earlier lines twice. Resolve all item references and validate the combined demand per stock under lock before applying any updates.

findings.title: Malformed quantities are silently accepted
findings.detail: After the parser panic is fixed, ignoring strconv.Atoi errors will let a mistyped quantity become zero and be silently skipped by ReserveLines. An out-of-range quantity can also be accepted at the integer limit. Return a parse error whenever Atoi fails so LoadOrder rejects the malformed order.

findings.title: Order files are left open
findings.detail: LoadOrder never closes the file after a successful os.Open. Repeated loads can accumulate open descriptors until garbage collection runs and cause otherwise valid opens to fail. Defer file.Close immediately after the open succeeds so every return path releases the descriptor.

findings.title: Concurrent cache reads and writes can crash the process
findings.detail: Get reads the entries map without taking the mutex that Put holds while writing. A lookup concurrent with a write can terminate the process with a concurrent map read/write error.

findings.title: Cache misses on fresh entries and serves expired values
findings.detail: Get returns a miss when the expiration is in the future and returns the stored value at or after expiration. With a positive TTL, a fresh entry misses immediately and becomes readable once it is stale.

findings.title: Expired cache entries accumulate without a bound
findings.detail: Neither Get nor Put removes expired keys. Even after correcting the expiration check, a long-lived cache that sees a steady stream of distinct keys retains them for its lifetime and can eventually exhaust process memory.

findings.title: Release accepts counts that corrupt stock balances
findings.detail: Releasing more units than are reserved makes Reserved negative, so Free reports more than the fixed capacity and a later Reserve can accept an oversized reservation. A negative release count instead increases Reserved and can take it above capacity.

findings.title: Release can lose concurrent order reservation updates
findings.detail: The new Release method updates Reserved under the stock mutex, but ReserveLines updates the same field at stock.go:42 without acquiring that mutex. If an order reservation and a release overlap on the same stock, one update can overwrite the other and leave the available quantity incorrect.

findings.title: Cache.Get treats expired entries as fresh and fresh entries as misses
findings.detail: The check `if found.expires.After(cache.Now()) { return 0, false }` is backwards. While an entry is still valid (its expiry is in the future), `Get` reports a miss. After the TTL has passed, it returns the cached value as a hit. Every lookup made within the TTL misses, and every lookup made after it gets a stale value without any sign that it is stale, which is the opposite of what a cache should do. Smallest fix: return a miss when `!found.expires.After(cache.Now())`, i.e. when `cache.Now()` is at or after `expires`.

findings.title: Cache.Get reads the map without the mutex
findings.detail: `Put` takes `cache.mutex` before writing to `entries`, but `Get` reads `cache.entries[key]` without taking it. A `Get` running at the same time as a `Put` is a data race, and the Go runtime may stop the process with "concurrent map read and map write". The type has a mutex, so it is clearly meant to be used concurrently. Smallest fix: add `cache.mutex.Lock(); defer cache.mutex.Unlock()` at the start of `Get`.

findings.title: Release accepts any count and can push Reserved below zero
findings.detail: `Release` subtracts `count` without checking it. A double release, a release larger than what was reserved, or a negative count leaves `Reserved` negative (or increases it). `Free()` then reports more free units than `Capacity`, and `Reserve` lets the item be oversold, with nothing to show the numbers are wrong. `Reserve` already rejects counts that are not positive. Smallest fix: under the lock, reject `count <= 0` and `count > stock.Reserved` and return an error, the same way `Reserve` does.

findings.title: Expiry check is inverted: live entries miss, expired entries hit
findings.detail: Get returns a miss when `found.expires.After(cache.Now())`, which is true for an entry that has not expired yet. So a fresh entry is never returned, and an expired one is returned as a valid hit. Every caller gets stale values once the TTL passes and never gets fresh ones. The condition should be `!found.expires.After(cache.Now())`.

findings.title: Get reads the map without taking the mutex, racing with Put
findings.detail: Put locks cache.mutex while it writes entries, but Get reads cache.entries without locking. If one goroutine calls Get while another calls Put, that is a data race on a Go map. The runtime can abort with 'fatal error: concurrent map read and map write', or Get can return a corrupted result. Get must lock and unlock the mutex the same way Put does.

findings.title: Release does not validate count, so Reserved can go negative or grow
findings.detail: Release subtracts count with no checks. If count is larger than Reserved (for example a double release or a wrong amount), Reserved becomes negative and Free() reports more units than Capacity, which allows overselling. A negative count instead increases Reserved and bypasses the capacity check in Reserve. Release should reject count <= 0 and count > Reserved, as Reserve does for its own input.

findings.title: Expired entries are never evicted, so the cache grows without bound
findings.detail: No code ever removes entries from the map: Get does not delete an expired entry, and there is no cleanup sweep. When keys are many or keep changing, memory grows for the life of the process.

findings.title: Cache reads accept expired values and reject fresh ones
findings.detail: Get treats an expiration time in the future as a miss and returns the stored value at or after expiration. A lookup can silently use stale data while fresh entries are ignored. Return a miss when the expiration time is at or before the current time.

findings.title: Concurrent cache reads and writes can crash the process
findings.detail: Get reads the entries map without acquiring the mutex that Put holds while writing to it. A lookup overlapping a cache fill can crash the process. Acquire the same mutex before reading the map.

findings.title: Release can corrupt the reserved stock count
findings.detail: Release subtracts the count unconditionally. For example, releasing a reservation twice can drive Reserved below zero, so Free reports more than the fixed capacity and Reserve can accept more units than exist. A negative count also increases Reserved. While holding the mutex, reject negative counts and counts greater than Reserved, leaving stock unchanged and returning an error.

findings.title: Export allows shell command injection
findings.detail: Export interpolates all three arguments into a command passed to `sh -c`. Shell syntax in a path or a quote in the pattern can change the command. If a caller passes untrusted input, it can run arbitrary commands with the process's privileges.

findings.title: Export misinterprets paths containing spaces or wildcards
findings.detail: The shell splits unquoted paths at spaces and expands wildcard characters. Export can fail on a valid filename or read and write paths other than the ones the caller supplied.

findings.title: Export lets grep interpret operands as options
findings.detail: Export passes the pattern and stock filename without establishing where grep options end. A pattern beginning with a hyphen can be rejected as an option or change grep's behavior. A relative stock filename beginning with a hyphen can also be parsed as an option.

findings.title: Export truncates files before checking whether grep can succeed
findings.detail: The shell truncates the report before grep opens the stock file. If both paths refer to the same file, Export destroys the stock data. A missing stock file or invalid pattern can also erase a previous report before Export reports the error.

findings.title: Export reports an empty match set as an error
findings.detail: Grep returns status 1 when it finds no matches. The resulting empty report is correct, but Export returns an error and makes callers handle a normal search result as a failure.

findings.title: Page discards the final partial page
findings.detail: With five items and a page size of three, page 1 should contain the last two items. The upper bound exceeds the slice length, so Page returns nil and drops those items.

findings.title: Page offset overflow can panic or return the wrong items
findings.detail: Both offset calculations can overflow an int. For example, `number = MaxInt` and `size = 1` wrap the end offset to a negative value, which passes the length check and panics during slicing. Other wrapped offsets can select items from an earlier page.

findings.title: Retry reports success after exhausting failed attempts
findings.detail: Retry records each failure in `last` but returns nil after exhausting the attempts. Callers can proceed as though work succeeded even though every call failed. A nonpositive attempt count also returns nil without calling work.

findings.title: Retry waits after the final failed attempt
findings.detail: Retry sleeps after the final failed call even though there is no next attempt. A single failed attempt therefore incurs the full configured pause before the caller gets control back.

findings.title: Retry returns nil after all attempts fail
findings.detail: The loop exits after every attempt has failed, then runs `return nil` instead of `return last`. The doc comment promises the last error. As written, a persistent failure looks like success to the caller, who then goes ahead on work that never happened. Fix: `return last`. Related: the function also sleeps after the final failed attempt for no reason. Skip `time.Sleep` when `attempt == attempts-1`.

findings.title: Shell command built from unescaped arguments allows injection and breaks on ordinary input
findings.detail: `Export` runs `sh -c "grep '"+pattern+"' "+stockFile+" > "+report`. A pattern that contains a single quote (for example `O'Neil`) either breaks the command or lets the caller's text run arbitrary shell commands. A file name with spaces or shell metacharacters goes wrong the same way, and the `>` redirect can overwrite an unintended file. Also, grep exits with status 1 when nothing matches, so an export with no matches is reported as an error. Fix: drop the shell. Run `exec.Command("grep", "-e", pattern, "--", stockFile)` and set its Stdout to a file opened with `os.Create(report)`. Treat exit code 1 as an empty result rather than an error. Better still, read the file and match the lines in Go.

findings.title: Last partial page is silently dropped
findings.detail: When `end > len(items)`, the function returns nil. Any page that is not completely full therefore comes back empty: with 10 items and size 3, page 3 should return items[9:10] but returns nil. Callers lose items without any sign. Fix: return nil only when `start >= len(items)`; otherwise clamp with `end = min(end, len(items))` and return `items[start:end]`. Separately, `number*size` can overflow for very large values; the check `number > len(items)/size` guards against that.

findings.title: Shell command injection through pattern, stockFile and report
findings.detail: Export joins pattern, stockFile and report straight into a string and runs it with `sh -c`. A pattern that contains a single quote (for example `x'; rm -rf ~; echo '`), or a file name that contains spaces, `;`, `$()` or `>`, runs any command the caller chooses, or sends output to a different file. Call exec.Command("grep", "--", pattern, stockFile) directly, without a shell, and write its stdout to a file opened in Go. Also, grep exits with status 1 when no line matches, so Export returns an error for an empty result.

findings.title: Retry returns nil when every attempt failed
findings.detail: The function ends with `return nil` instead of `return last`. When work fails on every attempt, the caller is told it succeeded and goes on as if the operation had happened, so failures are lost silently. This goes against the doc comment, which says it returns the last error.

findings.title: The last, partial page is dropped
findings.detail: When end > len(items), Page returns nil instead of clamping end to len(items). Unless len(items) is an exact multiple of size, the items on the last page can never be reached. For example, with 5 items and size 2, page 2 returns nil instead of [item4]. Return nil only when start >= len(items), and otherwise set end = min(end, len(items)). In addition, number*size can overflow for very large inputs, which gives a negative start and a slice panic.

findings.title: Sleeps after the final failed attempt
findings.detail: time.Sleep(pause) also runs after the last attempt, so the caller waits a full pause for nothing before it gets the result. There is also no context, so a caller cannot cancel a long retry loop.

findings.title: Export interprets caller input as shell code
findings.detail: Export interpolates the pattern and both paths into `sh -c`. A quote in a pattern or a space in a filename can break an ordinary export, and shell syntax in any argument can change the command or execute another one with the caller's permissions. Invoke grep directly with `-e` for the pattern and pass the stock and report files through stdin and stdout.

findings.title: A failed export can erase an existing report
findings.detail: The shell opens and truncates the report before grep validates the pattern or reads the stock file. An invalid pattern can erase an existing report, and using the stock file itself as the destination can erase the inventory. Reject destinations that refer to the stock file, write to a temporary file beside the report, and replace the report only after grep completes successfully.

findings.title: Retry reports success when every attempt fails
findings.detail: After every attempt fails, Retry discards `last` and returns nil. A caller can treat an operation that never succeeded as complete. Return `last` after the loop.

findings.title: Pagination silently drops the final partial page
findings.detail: Page returns nil when the requested page starts inside the slice but ends beyond it. With 11 items and a page size of 10, page 1 silently omits the eleventh item. Return nil when the start is out of range and clamp the page length to the number of items remaining.

findings.title: Retry waits after its last attempt
findings.detail: Retry sleeps after its final failed call, even though there is no next attempt. With one attempt it still waits the full pause before returning. Sleep only when another attempt remains.

findings.title: Large page offsets can overflow
findings.detail: The page offsets are computed before checking bounds. Large positive inputs can overflow `int`, causing a slice panic or selecting the wrong page. For a nonempty slice, check `number` against `(len(items)-1)/size` before multiplying and bound the page length by `len(items)-start` before adding.

findings.title: ParseLine panics with index out of range on every valid line
findings.detail: The note loop runs `for index := 2; index <= len(fields); index++` and reads fields[index]. For a plain "item;3" line, len(fields) is 2, so the first pass reads fields[2] and panics. The `<=` reads one past the end for every line with two or more fields, so LoadOrder crashes on any real order file. Fix: use `index < len(fields)`, or drop the unused note loop entirely (note is thrown away with `_ = note`).

findings.title: A quantity that isn't a number becomes 0 and the line is silently dropped
findings.detail: `quantity, _ := strconv.Atoi(...)` throws away the parse error. A typo such as "widget;1O" or an empty field gives Quantity 0, and ReserveLines then skips any line with Quantity == 0. The order is accepted but missing that line, and nothing reports it. Negative values are also accepted. Fix: return an error when Atoi fails or when quantity <= 0.

findings.title: ReserveLines skips the capacity check, the count check and the lock
findings.detail: ReserveLines does `stock.Reserved += line.Quantity` directly instead of calling Reserve. That skips three things Reserve enforces. Without the capacity check, Reserved can exceed Capacity, so Free() goes negative and the stock is oversold. Without the positive-count check, a negative quantity reduces Reserved. Without the mutex, this write races with Reserve and Free, and concurrent updates can be lost. Fix: call `stock.Reserve(line.Quantity)` for each line and return its error.

findings.title: A failure partway through leaves the earlier lines reserved
findings.detail: If a later line names an unknown item (or, once F3 is fixed, has too little stock), ReserveLines returns an error. The lines before it have already been reserved and are not undone. Retrying the order then reserves them a second time. Fix: check every line first (item exists, enough free stock) before changing anything, or undo the reservations already made when a line fails.

findings.title: LoadOrder never closes the file
findings.detail: The file returned by os.Open is never closed, so every call leaks a file descriptor. Fix: add `defer file.Close()` right after the error check.

findings.title: ParseLine note loop indexes past the end of fields and panics on every line
findings.detail: The loop runs `for index := 2; index <= len(fields); index++` and reads fields[index]. When index == len(fields), the read is out of range. A plain "item;3" line has len(fields)==2, so it reads fields[2] and panics right away. Every line with a note panics on its last step too. As written, every valid order line panics: index out of range. The bound should be `<`.

findings.title: Quantity parse error is ignored, so malformed quantities silently become 0
findings.detail: `quantity, _ := strconv.Atoi(...)` throws away the error. Input like "apple;x" or "apple;" parses as Quantity 0 with no error, and ReserveLines then skips it. A corrupted order line is dropped silently instead of being rejected.

findings.title: ReserveLines writes stock.Reserved without taking the mutex (data race)
findings.detail: ReserveLines changes stock.Reserved directly and never locks stock.mutex. Reserve and Free do lock it. If ReserveLines runs at the same time as Reserve, Free or another ReserveLines on the same Stock, that is a data race and updates can be lost. It should call stock.Reserve or take the lock.

findings.title: ReserveLines skips the capacity check and can over-reserve
findings.detail: Unlike Reserve, ReserveLines never checks Reserved+Quantity against Capacity. An order for more than the free stock pushes Reserved past Capacity, Free() goes negative, and no ErrNotEnough is returned.

findings.title: Negative quantities are accepted and reduce Reserved
findings.detail: ParseLine accepts "item;-5". ReserveLines only skips a quantity of exactly 0, so a negative quantity is added to Reserved and lowers it. That releases stock that other orders hold and inflates Free(). Reserve rejects count <= 0, but this path does not.

findings.title: Partial reservation is left in place when a later line fails
findings.detail: Lines are applied one at a time. If a later line names an unknown item, the function returns an error but keeps the reservations already made for the earlier lines. The caller sees the order as failed while stock stays reserved for it, so units leak.

findings.title: LoadOrder never closes the opened file
findings.detail: os.Open is never paired with file.Close (no defer). Every call leaks a file descriptor, on success and on the early return after a parse error. A long-running process will eventually run out of descriptors.

findings.title: Lines longer than 64KB make LoadOrder fail
findings.detail: bufio.Scanner uses the default 64KB token limit. A longer line (for example one with a long note) stops the scan with bufio.ErrTooLong and the whole order fails to load.

findings.title: Every valid order line panics
findings.detail: The note loop uses `index <= len(fields)`, so every line with at least two fields eventually indexes `fields[len(fields)]` and panics. Any order containing a valid line therefore fails to load. Remove the loop because the parsed result does not use the note.

findings.title: Order reservations can corrupt stock counts
findings.detail: Directly incrementing `Reserved` lets an order exceed capacity, reduce existing reservations with a negative quantity, or silently skip a zero quantity. Apply the same positive-quantity and capacity checks as `Stock.Reserve` and propagate the error, comparing the requested quantity against free stock before adding.

findings.title: Invalid quantities are accepted silently
findings.detail: Once the parser panic is fixed, ignoring `strconv.Atoi` errors will allow malformed quantities to become zero and out-of-range quantities to become integer limits. An order with a mistyped quantity can then load successfully with the wrong count. Return the conversion error with the offending quantity.

findings.title: Order reservations bypass stock synchronization
findings.detail: `ReserveLines` writes `Reserved` without acquiring the mutex used by `Stock.Reserve` and `Stock.Free`. Concurrent calls can race, and competing reservations can lose an update. Route each update through `Stock.Reserve` or hold the same mutex when validating and updating the stock.

findings.title: A failed order leaves earlier lines reserved
findings.detail: When an unknown item appears after a valid line, `ReserveLines` returns an error but leaves the earlier reservation in place. Correcting the item and retrying can reserve the earlier line twice. Resolve all item names before changing stock, and perform any stock validation that can fail before committing the updates.

findings.title: Loading orders leaks file descriptors
findings.detail: `LoadOrder` never closes the file after a successful `os.Open`. Repeated loads can exhaust the process's file descriptors. Defer `file.Close()` immediately after checking the open error.

findings.title: Parsing any valid order line panics
findings.detail: The note loop reaches index len(fields), which is outside the slice. Every line with at least two fields panics, including valid lines with and without a note. LoadOrder hits the same panic when it reads a valid order.

findings.title: Invalid quantities are accepted as successful parses
findings.detail: Once the parser panic is fixed, ignoring the Atoi error will accept malformed quantities as zero and out-of-range quantities as a saturated integer. LoadOrder will report these corrupted quantities as successfully parsed.

findings.title: Loading an order leaks its file descriptor
findings.detail: After os.Open succeeds, the file is never explicitly closed. Successful reads and early failures leave descriptors open until garbage collection, so repeated calls can exhaust the process's descriptor limit.

findings.title: Order reservations race with other stock operations
findings.detail: ReserveLines writes Reserved without taking the stock mutex. Concurrent calls involving the same stock race with each other and with Reserve or Free. Concurrent updates can lose reservations.

findings.title: Orders can reserve more stock than is available
findings.detail: The unchecked addition can push Reserved beyond Capacity and still return success. Duplicate lines can exceed capacity cumulatively, and sufficiently large quantities can wrap Reserved. Free then reports incorrect availability.

findings.title: Order reservations accept nonpositive quantities
findings.detail: A negative quantity decreases Reserved and can make Free report more units than Capacity. A zero quantity is silently skipped. Both quantities violate the positive-count rule enforced by Stock.Reserve.

findings.title: An unknown item leaves the order partially reserved
findings.detail: An unknown item causes an error after any preceding lines have already updated their stocks. The caller receives only the error, so retrying the order after correcting the unknown item can reserve the earlier lines twice.

findings.title: A nil stock entry panics during reservation
findings.detail: A map entry with a nil *Stock passes the presence check. A line with a nonzero quantity then dereferences the nil pointer and panics.

findings.title: The loader rejects valid lines with long notes
findings.detail: The scanner uses its default token limit of roughly 64 KiB. A line with a sufficiently long optional note exceeds that limit and makes LoadOrder return a scan error, even though the documented line format specifies no length limit.

findings.title: Expiry check is inverted, so Get returns expired values and misses valid ones
findings.detail: `if found.expires.After(cache.Now()) { return 0, false }` treats an entry as a miss while it is still valid (its expiry is in the future). Once the TTL has passed, it returns the old value as a hit. Every call within the TTL misses, and every call after it returns stale data with no warning. Fix: `if !found.expires.After(cache.Now()) { return 0, false }`, or equivalently `if cache.Now().After(found.expires)`.

findings.title: Get reads the map without holding the mutex
findings.detail: Put locks cache.mutex but Get doesn't, so reading the map in Get races with the write in Put. In Go, a map read and write at the same time is a fatal runtime error ("concurrent map read and map write") that stops the whole process, and the race detector will flag it. A cache that holds a mutex is clearly meant to be used from several goroutines at once. Fix: add `cache.mutex.Lock(); defer cache.mutex.Unlock()` at the top of Get.

findings.title: Release accepts counts that make Reserved negative
findings.detail: Release subtracts count with no checks. A double release, or a count larger than Reserved, pushes Reserved below zero. Free() then reports more units than Capacity, and later Reserve calls succeed beyond the real stock, which is overselling that goes unnoticed. A negative count also quietly adds to Reserved. Reserve already rejects counts that are zero or negative. Fix: return an error, and leave Reserved unchanged, when count <= 0 or count > stock.Reserved.

findings.title: Expiry check inverted: live entries miss, expired entries hit
findings.detail: Get returns a miss when `found.expires.After(cache.Now())`, which is exactly when the entry is still valid. Once the TTL has passed, it returns the value as a hit. So every fresh Put is never served, and stale values are served forever. The condition should be `!found.expires.After(cache.Now())`.

findings.title: Get reads the map without holding the mutex, racing Put
findings.detail: Put locks cache.mutex before it writes cache.entries, but Get reads cache.entries with no lock. If Get and Put run at the same time on different goroutines, that is a data race, and Go's runtime can stop the process with 'concurrent map read and map write'. Get should lock the mutex as Put does.

findings.title: Release does not validate count, so Reserved can go negative
findings.detail: Release subtracts any count with no checks. A negative count adds reserved units with no capacity check. A count larger than Reserved, such as a double release, makes Reserved negative, so Free() returns more than Capacity and later reservations can oversell. Release should reject count <= 0 and count > Reserved, as Reserve does with its own checks.

findings.title: Expired entries are never removed, so the cache grows without bound
findings.detail: No code ever deletes an entry. Get does not drop expired entries and there is no sweep, so the map keeps every key ever put. With many distinct keys, memory use grows without limit.

findings.title: Cache misses fresh entries and serves expired ones
findings.detail: Get returns a miss while the expiration is in the future, then returns the cached value at and after expiration. Normal lookups miss fresh values and can silently use stale ones. Reject the entry when its expiration is at or before the current time.

findings.title: Concurrent cache reads and writes can crash the process
findings.detail: Get reads the map without taking the mutex used by Put. A lookup that overlaps a cache fill can terminate the Go process with a concurrent map read and write error, interrupting in-flight work. Take the same mutex around the map lookup.

findings.title: Invalid releases can corrupt stock totals
findings.detail: Release subtracts any count. A duplicate release can drive Reserved below zero, so Free reports more than Capacity and Reserve can accept orders beyond physical stock. A negative count instead increases Reserved without checking capacity. Validate both bounds under the mutex and report invalid releases without changing stock.

findings.title: Reserving an order while releasing stock can lose an update
findings.detail: ReserveLines already updates Reserved without locking. With the new Release method, an order reservation and a cancellation for the same item can overwrite each other's updates even though Release takes the mutex. Protect the ReserveLines increment with the same stock mutex.

findings.title: The cache misses fresh entries and returns expired entries
findings.detail: The expiration check is inverted. A lookup misses while the expiration time is in the future, then starts returning the stored value at the expiration time and continues serving it indefinitely.

findings.title: Concurrent cache reads and writes can crash the process
findings.detail: Get reads the map without taking the mutex that Put holds while writing. Concurrent calls on the same cache race even for different keys and can terminate the process with a concurrent map read and write error.

findings.title: Expired entries accumulate without bound
findings.detail: Neither Put nor Get removes expired entries. A long-lived cache that sees new keys keeps every distinct key and value reachable, so memory can grow until the process runs out.

findings.title: Unchecked release counts corrupt inventory
findings.detail: Release subtracts any count. A duplicate release or a count larger than Reserved can make Reserved negative, causing Free to exceed Capacity and allowing later reservations beyond physical stock. A negative count instead increases Reserved without the checks in Reserve.

findings.title: Releasing stock can lose a concurrent order reservation
findings.detail: Release updates Reserved under the stock mutex, but ReserveLines updates the same field directly. When these two operations overlap on the same Stock, their read-modify-write operations race and can lose either the reservation or the release.

findings.title: Retry reports success when every attempt fails
findings.detail: The function ends with `return nil` rather than `return last`. When all attempts fail, it reports success, which contradicts its doc comment. Callers will continue as if the work had succeeded (for example, a save that never happened), and nothing will show the failure. Fix: `return last`. Also, skip the sleep after the final attempt so it doesn't add a pointless delay.

findings.title: Shell command injection and broken quoting in Export
findings.detail: `pattern`, `stockFile` and `report` are joined into a string run by `sh -c`. A pattern that contains `'` (for example "O'Brien") breaks the command. A crafted pattern such as `'; rm -rf ~; '` runs any command, and file names with spaces or shell metacharacters are interpreted by the shell too. A redirect into the wrong path can also truncate an unrelated file. There is a second problem: grep exits with status 1 when nothing matches, so an empty result is reported as an error. Fix: don't use the shell. Use `exec.Command("grep", "-e", pattern, "--", stockFile)` with `cmd.Stdout` set to a file created by `os.Create(report)`, and treat exit code 1 as no matches. Better still, filter the lines in Go with bufio and strings/regexp.

findings.title: Last partial page is silently dropped
findings.detail: When `end > len(items)`, the function returns nil instead of shortening the slice. Whenever len(items) isn't a multiple of size, the items on the last partial page can never be reached. For example, 25 items with size 10 gives page 2 as nil, so 5 items disappear and no error shows it. Fix: return nil only when `start >= len(items)`, and otherwise set `end = min(end, len(items))`. Also consider guarding against overflow in `number*size` for very large inputs.

findings.title: Shell command injection through pattern, stockFile and report
findings.detail: Export builds a shell command by joining pattern, stockFile and report into a string and runs it with `sh -c`. Single quotes around pattern are the only guard. A pattern such as `x'; rm -rf ~; echo '` breaks out of the quotes, and stockFile or report can carry `;`, `$(...)` or backticks with no quoting at all. Any caller that passes user input therefore lets that user run arbitrary commands. The fix is to call exec.Command("grep", "--", pattern, stockFile) and write its stdout to a file opened in Go.

findings.title: Retry returns nil when every attempt failed
findings.detail: After the loop ends with every call failing, the function returns nil instead of `last`. This contradicts its doc comment. Callers are told the work succeeded when it never did, so failures are silently swallowed.

findings.title: Last partial page is dropped
findings.detail: When end > len(items), Page returns nil instead of clamping end to len(items). Example: with 5 items and size 2, page 2 should return [item5] but returns nil. Any trailing items that do not fill a whole page can never be reached.

findings.title: Sleeps needlessly after the final failed attempt
findings.detail: time.Sleep(pause) also runs after the last attempt, so a call that has already failed for good is delayed by an extra pause before it returns.

findings.title: Integer overflow in number*size for large inputs
findings.detail: With very large number or size values, start := number*size and end := start+size can overflow and wrap to a negative or small value. The bounds check then passes and items[start:end] either panics with a slice-out-of-range error or returns the wrong page.

findings.title: No-match and failure leave a truncated report and a misleading error
findings.detail: The shell redirect creates or truncates the report file before grep runs. grep exits with status 1 when nothing matches, so a legitimate empty result comes back as an error, and a failed run still leaves an empty or overwritten report behind.

findings.title: Returned page aliases the caller's backing array
findings.detail: items[start:end] keeps the spare capacity of items. If a caller appends to the returned page, it overwrites the items that follow in the original slice. A full slice expression, items[start:end:end], avoids this.

findings.title: Retry reports success after exhausting all attempts
findings.detail: At retry.go:15, Retry returns nil after every attempt fails. Callers can proceed as if a stock operation succeeded even though it never did. Return last after the loop.

findings.title: Page silently drops the final partial page
findings.detail: At page.go:10, Page returns nil whenever the requested page extends past the end of the slice. With five items and a page size of two, the third page silently omits the fifth item. Return nil only when the page starts at or beyond the end, and clamp the end to len(items).

findings.title: Export interprets input as shell code
findings.detail: At export.go:8, Export inserts all three arguments into shell source. Paths containing spaces can be split, apostrophes in a pattern can break quoting, and crafted arguments can execute commands with the caller's privileges. Invoke grep directly, pass the pattern with -e and the input path after --, and connect stdout to a file opened by Go.

findings.title: A failed export can erase the previous report
findings.detail: At export.go:8, redirection truncates an existing report before grep checks whether it can read the stock file or compile the pattern. A failed rerun can erase the previous report. Write to a temporary file in the report directory and replace the destination only after the export completes successfully.

findings.title: Page arithmetic can overflow and panic
findings.detail: At page.go:8–13, large nonnegative arguments can overflow the offset or end calculation. The length check can then pass with invalid slice bounds and Page can panic. Check whether the page number is in range before multiplying, and cap the page length to the remaining items before adding.

findings.title: Retry waits after the final attempt
findings.detail: At retry.go:13, Retry sleeps after the final failed call, delaying the result by a full pause even when attempts is one. Sleep only when another attempt remains.

findings.title: Export lets caller input alter the shell command
findings.detail: Export interpolates the pattern and both paths into a shell command. Shell syntax in any caller-controlled argument can execute commands with the process's privileges. Ordinary inputs also break, including paths with spaces and patterns with apostrophes.

findings.title: Export can erase its stock file
findings.detail: The shell truncates the report before grep opens the stock file. If both paths refer to the same file, including through a hard link or symlink, Export erases the stock data before reading it.

findings.title: Export misinterprets patterns and filenames that begin with a dash
findings.detail: A pattern beginning with a dash can be parsed as a grep option because Export does not mark it with -e. An option-looking stock filename can also change grep's behavior, and a filename of '-' makes grep read standard input.

findings.title: Export reports an error when there are no matches
findings.detail: When no lines match, grep creates the expected empty report and exits with status 1. Export returns that status as an error, so callers cannot distinguish a valid empty result from a failed export without inspecting the exit status themselves.

findings.title: Page drops the final partial page
findings.detail: Page returns nil whenever the requested end exceeds the item count, even when the start is within the slice. With three items and a page size of two, page one omits the third item.

findings.title: Page can panic when its index arithmetic overflows
findings.detail: Large positive inputs can overflow either the multiplication that computes the start or the addition that computes the end. A wrapped end can pass the length check, leading to a slice-bounds panic or a result from the wrong offset.

findings.title: Retry reports success after all attempts fail
findings.detail: After all attempts fail, Retry discards the last error and returns nil. Callers can then proceed as though work succeeded even though every invocation failed.

findings.title: Retry waits after the last attempt
findings.detail: Retry sleeps for the full pause after the final failed call, even with a single configured attempt. This delays the return by one interval beyond the documented waits between calls.

findings.title: Note loop reads past the end of fields and panics on every line
findings.detail: The loop runs `for index := 2; index <= len(fields); index++` and reads fields[index]. When index == len(fields) this is out of range. Any valid input such as "apple;3" (len 2) or "apple;3;gift" (len 3) triggers an index-out-of-range panic, so ParseLine and LoadOrder crash on every well-formed line.

findings.title: ReserveLines skips the capacity check and allows overselling
findings.detail: ReserveLines does `stock.Reserved += line.Quantity` directly and never calls Reserve. It never checks Reserved+count <= Capacity, so Reserved can go above Capacity, Free() becomes negative, and stock is oversold.

findings.title: Data race: Reserved is changed without taking the stock mutex
findings.detail: Reserve and Free take stock.mutex, but ReserveLines reads and writes stock.Reserved without locking. If ReserveLines runs at the same time as Reserve, Free or another ReserveLines on the same Stock, updates are lost and the race detector reports a data race.

findings.title: Bad quantity is silently parsed as 0 and the line is dropped
findings.detail: The strconv.Atoi error is thrown away. A quantity such as "abc", "" or "3.5" becomes 0 with no error. ReserveLines then skips lines whose quantity is 0, so a malformed order line is silently not reserved and the order is reported as successful.

findings.title: Negative quantities are accepted and lower Reserved
findings.detail: Nothing rejects a negative quantity. A line such as "apple;-5" parses fine and ReserveLines adds -5 to Reserved. This releases stock that other orders hold and can push Reserved below zero. Reserve rejects count <= 0, but ReserveLines does not.

findings.title: Order is partly reserved when it fails partway
findings.detail: Lines are reserved one at a time. When a later line names an unknown item, the function returns an error, but the earlier lines stay reserved and are never rolled back. The caller sees a failed order, yet some stock stays reserved and leaks.

findings.title: Order file is never closed (file descriptor leak)
findings.detail: os.Open is called but there is no file.Close (no defer) on any path, including error returns from ParseLine. Each call leaks a file descriptor, so a long-running process eventually hits the open-file limit.

findings.title: Lines over 64 KiB make the whole load fail
findings.detail: bufio.Scanner uses its default 64 KiB token limit. A longer line, for example one with a long note, stops scanning with bufio.ErrTooLong, and the whole order fails to load.

findings.title: Every valid order line panics
findings.detail: The note loop reads fields[len(fields)] for every line with at least two fields. Both documented formats therefore panic, and LoadOrder cannot load a valid nonempty order. Remove the loop since Line does not use the note.

findings.title: Orders can overbook stock or undo reservations
findings.detail: ReserveLines adds quantities directly to Reserved and returns success even when the order exceeds available stock. Negative quantities can also reduce existing reservations. Use Stock.Reserve for each line and propagate its errors. Make its capacity check compare the count against remaining capacity so the addition cannot overflow.

findings.title: Reservation updates bypass the stock mutex
findings.detail: ReserveLines updates Reserved without taking the mutex used by Reserve and Free. Concurrent calls on the same stock race and can lose reservation updates while reporting success. Route the update through Stock.Reserve or hold the same mutex across validation and mutation.

findings.title: A failed order can leave stock reserved
findings.detail: If a later item is unknown, ReserveLines returns an error after mutating stock for earlier lines. Correcting the item and retrying the order reserves those earlier lines again. Resolve all item lookups before mutating stock. If capacity checks can also fail, validate the whole order under the relevant stock locks before applying it.

findings.title: Invalid quantities are accepted as valid orders
findings.detail: Once the parser panic is fixed, ignoring strconv.Atoi errors lets a blank or malformed quantity become zero and be silently skipped by ReserveLines. An out-of-range quantity can become a saturated integer. Return a parse error for failed conversions and reject nonpositive quantities.

findings.title: Loading orders leaks file descriptors
findings.detail: LoadOrder opens the input and leaves it open on success and on parsing or scanning errors. Repeated loads can exhaust file descriptors before garbage collection closes the files. Defer file.Close immediately after the successful open.

findings.title: Parsing any well-formed order line panics
findings.detail: The loop runs with index equal to len(fields) and reads fields[index]. Every line with at least two fields panics, including a valid line without a note. LoadOrder inherits the panic.

findings.title: Invalid quantities are silently accepted
findings.detail: The parser discards the error from strconv.Atoi. Once the preceding panic is fixed, blank or nonnumeric quantities will be accepted as zero, and out-of-range quantities will be accepted as a saturated integer.

findings.title: Loading orders leaks file descriptors
findings.detail: A successful os.Open is never paired with Close. Calls leave descriptors open until garbage collection, including when the file is empty or parsing fails. Repeated loads can exhaust the process's file descriptors.

findings.title: Long notes prevent otherwise valid orders from loading
findings.detail: The default bufio.Scanner token limit rejects an otherwise valid order line whose optional note exceeds roughly 64 KiB. The documented line format has no length limit.

findings.title: Batch reservations race with other stock operations
findings.detail: ReserveLines modifies Reserved without taking the stock mutex used by Reserve and Free. Concurrent calls on the same stock can race, and concurrent reservations can lose updates.

findings.title: Orders can reserve more stock than is available
findings.detail: The function increments Reserved without checking available capacity. An order can reserve more units than are available, return success, and leave Free reporting a negative count.

findings.title: Batch reservations accept zero and negative quantities
findings.detail: Stock.Reserve rejects counts less than or equal to zero. ReserveLines silently skips zero and adds negative quantities to Reserved, which can release existing reservations and inflate available stock.

findings.title: A failed order can leave earlier lines reserved
findings.detail: When an unknown item appears after a valid line, the function returns an error with the earlier reservation still applied. The error gives the caller no way to determine how much of the order was applied, and retrying the order can reserve those units again.

findings.title: A nil stock entry crashes order reservation
findings.detail: The map lookup checks whether the key exists but does not check whether its value is nil. A nonzero line for an item mapped to nil panics when the function accesses Reserved.

findings.title: Note loop goes one past the end and crashes on every line
findings.detail: The loop is `for index := 2; index <= len(fields); index++ { note += fields[index] }`. It always reaches fields[len(fields)], which is out of range. For a plain `item;5` line, len is 2, so fields[2] crashes at once. A line with a note crashes on its last step. Every LoadOrder call on a file with any non-blank line therefore crashes. The note is thrown away anyway (`_ = note`). Smallest fix: delete the loop, or change the condition to `index < len(fields)`.

findings.title: ReserveLines skips Reserve's lock and capacity/sign checks
findings.detail: ReserveLines runs `stock.Reserved += line.Quantity` directly. It does not take stock.mutex, does not check Reserved+count against Capacity, and does not reject negative counts. Because of this, an order can reserve more than Capacity, so Free() goes negative and stock is overbooked without anyone noticing. A negative quantity in the file releases other orders' reservations. Running at the same time as Reserve is a data race. Fix: call `stock.Reserve(line.Quantity)` and return its error. Reserve already rejects counts <= 0, so drop the zero-skip or handle zero on purpose.

findings.title: Atoi error ignored; a bad quantity silently becomes 0
findings.detail: `quantity, _ := strconv.Atoi(...)` throws the error away. A typo such as `widget;1O` or `widget;` turns into quantity 0, and ReserveLines then skips that line, so the order is quietly under-reserved. Fix: return an error when Atoi fails, and reject quantities <= 0.

findings.title: A failed order leaves earlier lines reserved
