findings.detail: If a later line names an unknown item (or, after F2 is fixed, there is not enough stock), the function returns an error but keeps the reservations already made for earlier lines. The caller sees a failed order while the stock stays held. Fix: check all items before reserving anything, or undo the earlier reservations on error.

findings.title: File is never closed
findings.detail: LoadOrder never closes the file returned by os.Open, so each call leaks a file descriptor. Fix: add `defer file.Close()` after the error check.

findings.title: Expiry check is inverted: live entries miss, expired entries hit
findings.detail: Get returns a miss when found.expires.After(now), which is exactly when the entry is still valid, and returns the value once it has expired. Every lookup inside the TTL misses and every lookup after the TTL returns a stale value. The condition should be !found.expires.After(cache.Now()).

findings.title: Get reads the map without taking the mutex
findings.detail: Put writes cache.entries while holding cache.mutex, but Get reads the same map without locking. If Get and Put run at the same time, that is a data race on a Go map, and the runtime can abort with 'concurrent map read and map write'. Get needs to lock the mutex as Put does.

findings.title: Release accepts any count and can drive Reserved negative
findings.detail: Release subtracts count with no check: a count that is not positive, or larger than Reserved, is still subtracted. Releasing too much, or the same reservation twice, makes Reserved negative. Free() then reports more than Capacity, and Reserve lets callers take more units than exist. Reserve rejects count <= 0, but Release has no matching check.

findings.title: Expired entries are never removed
findings.detail: Nothing deletes an entry once it expires: Get does not remove it and there is no sweep. With many distinct keys, the entries map keeps growing for the life of the process, so memory is never released.

findings.title: Cache serves values only after they expire
findings.detail: `Cache.Get` returns a miss while the entry is fresh, then returns the stored value at and after expiration. Callers can silently use stale lookup results indefinitely. Reject the entry when its expiration is at or before the current time.

findings.title: Concurrent cache reads and writes can crash the process
findings.detail: `Cache.Get` reads the map without acquiring the mutex used by `Put`. A lookup that overlaps a cache update can terminate the Go process with a concurrent map read and write error. Acquire the same mutex around the lookup.

findings.title: Invalid releases can make unavailable stock reservable
findings.detail: `Release` subtracts the count unconditionally. Releasing more than is reserved makes `Reserved` negative, so `Free` can report more than capacity and `Reserve` can accept units that do not exist. A negative count increases `Reserved`. While holding the mutex, reject counts outside the range from zero through `Reserved` and leave the balance unchanged.

findings.title: Order reservations can race with stock releases
findings.detail: The new `Release` method locks around its update, but `ReserveLines` updates the same `Reserved` field without the lock. Reserving one order while releasing another for the same item can silently lose either update. Take the stock mutex around the existing increment in `ReserveLines` so both operations serialize.

findings.title: Cache rejects fresh entries and serves expired values
findings.detail: Get returns a miss while the expiration time is in the future, then returns the stored value at and after expiration. A positive-TTL entry is therefore unavailable during its intended lifetime and can be served stale indefinitely.

findings.title: Concurrent cache reads and writes can crash the process
findings.detail: Put locks the mutex before writing to entries, but Get reads the same map without locking. Concurrent calls can trigger a fatal concurrent map read and write error, even when they use different keys.

findings.title: Expired cache entries accumulate without bound
findings.detail: Expired entries stay in the map even when their keys are read again. A long-lived cache that sees a steady stream of distinct keys retains them all and can exhaust memory.

findings.title: Unchecked release counts corrupt stock availability
findings.detail: Releasing more units than are reserved, such as when a cancellation is processed twice, drives Reserved below zero. Free then reports more than Capacity and subsequent reservations can overbook stock. A negative release count increases Reserved without checking capacity.

findings.title: Releasing stock can race with reserving an order
findings.detail: Release locks the stock mutex, but ReserveLines updates Reserved directly without acquiring it. If an order reservation overlaps a release for the same item, the two read-modify-write operations can lose one update and leave availability incorrect.

findings.title: Expiry check is inverted: fresh entries miss, expired entries hit
findings.detail: `if found.expires.After(cache.Now()) { return 0, false }` treats an entry whose expiry is still in the future as a miss. Once the TTL has passed, it returns the stale value with ok=true. As a result the cache never serves a fresh value and always serves expired ones, so callers silently act on outdated lookups. Fix: use `if !found.expires.After(cache.Now())`, which is the same as `!cache.Now().Before(found.expires)`, to return the miss. Optionally delete the expired entry at the same point.

findings.title: Get reads the map without holding the mutex
findings.detail: Put locks cache.mutex before it writes to cache.entries, but Get reads cache.entries without locking. If one goroutine calls Get while another calls Put, that is a concurrent map read and write. The Go runtime detects this and stops the program with a fatal error ("concurrent map read and map write"), which a deferred recover cannot catch. The Cache type has a mutex, so it is clearly meant to be shared between goroutines. Fix: add `cache.mutex.Lock(); defer cache.mutex.Unlock()` at the top of Get.

findings.title: Release does not validate count, so Reserved can go negative
findings.detail: Reserve rejects a count that is not positive and refuses to go over Capacity. Release subtracts any count with no check. Releasing more than is reserved, for example by releasing twice after a retry, or passing a negative count corrupts the stock. Reserved becomes negative and Free() reports more units than Capacity, so later Reserve calls succeed beyond the real stock and the item is oversold without anyone noticing. Fix: return an error when count <= 0 or count > stock.Reserved, as Reserve already does for its inputs.

findings.title: Shell command injection through pattern and file names
findings.detail: Export builds a shell command by joining strings: "grep '"+pattern+"' "+stockFile+" > "+report, then runs it with sh -c. A pattern that contains a single quote, such as x'; rm -rf ~; echo ', ends the quoting and runs any command the caller puts after it. File names with spaces or shell metacharacters ($(), ;, |) are also run by the shell, and report can point the redirection at any file. Fix: run exec.Command("grep", "--", pattern, stockFile) with no shell, and write cmd.Stdout to a file opened in Go.

findings.title: Retry returns nil when every attempt failed
findings.detail: When the loop runs out of attempts it ends with `return nil` instead of `return last`. Every attempt can fail and the caller still sees success, which goes against the doc comment ('returns the last error when every call failed'). Failed operations are then treated as done.

findings.title: Last partial page is dropped
findings.detail: When end > len(items) the function returns nil instead of cutting end down to len(items). For example, 10 items with size 3 gives no page 3 (item 9 is lost). Any list whose length is not a multiple of size loses its last items. The check should be start >= len(items) → nil, and otherwise end = min(end, len(items)).

findings.title: Retry waits again after the last failed attempt
findings.detail: time.Sleep(pause) also runs after the last attempt fails, so the caller waits one extra pause for nothing before it gets the result.

findings.title: No matches is reported as an error
findings.detail: grep exits with status 1 when nothing matches, so Export returns an *exec.ExitError for a valid export that simply found no items. Callers cannot tell this apart from a real failure, such as a missing stock file (status 2). The redirection also creates or empties the report file even when grep fails.

findings.title: Export lets arguments control shell execution
findings.detail: Export interpolates the pattern and both paths into a shell command. Spaces and apostrophes in ordinary inputs can break the export, and shell syntax in any argument can execute commands with the caller’s permissions. Invoke grep directly, pass the pattern as a separate argument with `-e`, and connect the stock and report files through stdin and stdout.

findings.title: A failed export can erase an existing report
findings.detail: The shell opens and truncates the report before grep reads the stock file. A missing stock file or invalid pattern therefore destroys the previous report even though Export returns an error. Write to a temporary file in the report directory and replace the report only after grep and the output close succeed.

findings.title: Retry reports success after every attempt fails
findings.detail: When every callback invocation fails, Retry stores the last error and then returns nil. A caller can continue as if an inventory operation succeeded even though every attempt failed. Return `last` after the loop.

findings.title: Pagination silently drops the final partial page
findings.detail: When the final page contains fewer than `size` items, `end > len(items)` returns nil even though `start` points to valid items. For example, page 1 of 11 items at size 10 omits the eleventh item. Reject starts outside the list and cap the end at the list length.

findings.title: Large pagination arguments can panic
findings.detail: Large nonnegative page numbers or sizes can overflow `number * size` or `start + size`. A wrapped bound can pass the length check and panic when slicing. After handling an empty list, check `number <= (len(items)-1)/size` before multiplying, then limit the page length to `len(items)-start` before adding.

findings.title: Retry waits after the final failed attempt
findings.detail: Retry sleeps after the last failed call, adding the full pause before returning even when `attempts` is 1. Sleep only when another attempt remains.

findings.title: Export interprets caller-supplied text as shell code
findings.detail: Export concatenates all three arguments into a command interpreted by `sh -c`. Untrusted input can execute commands with the caller's privileges. Ordinary filenames containing spaces and patterns containing apostrophes can also be misparsed. Pass the pattern as a separate argument and handle the input and output files directly.

findings.title: Export lets grep interpret patterns and filenames as options
findings.detail: Quoting preserves a shell argument but does not stop grep from interpreting a leading hyphen as an option. A valid pattern such as `-draft` can be rejected or interpreted as flags. A stock filename beginning with a hyphen can also be consumed as an option. Pass the pattern with `-e` and open the stock file directly.

findings.title: Export can erase its own stock file
findings.detail: Shell redirection truncates the report before grep opens the stock file. If both paths refer to the same file, including through a filesystem alias, Export destroys the source data before reading it. Stage the output in a separate file before replacing the destination.

findings.title: A failed export can destroy an existing report
findings.detail: The same redirection destroys an existing report even when grep cannot perform the export, such as when the stock file is missing or the regular expression is invalid. Stage the new report and replace the old one only after grep completes successfully.

findings.title: Export reports an error when nothing matches
findings.detail: Grep exits with status 1 when it finds zero matching lines. `command.Run()` forwards that status as an error even though the empty report is the correct result. Handle grep's no-match status as a successful empty export.

findings.title: Page drops the final partial page
findings.detail: The `end > len(items)` check returns nil even when `start` points to an existing item. For five items and a page size of two, page 2 omits the fifth item. Reject starts at or beyond the slice length and clamp the end to the slice length.

findings.title: Page can panic when index arithmetic overflows
findings.detail: The offset multiplication and end addition can overflow before the bounds check. For example, a page number of `MaxInt` and a size of 1 wrap `end` to a negative value, which passes the check and panics during slicing. Bound the page number before multiplying and derive the end from the remaining slice length.

findings.title: Retry reports success after exhausting all attempts
findings.detail: After every call to `work` fails, Retry discards the final error and returns nil. Callers therefore receive a success result even though the operation never succeeded. Return `last` after the loop.

findings.title: Retry waits after the last failed attempt
findings.detail: Retry sleeps after the final failure even though no further call will occur. With one attempt, a failure delays the return by the full pause. Sleep only when another attempt remains.

findings.title: Retry returns nil after every attempt failed
findings.detail: After the loop ends, the function returns `nil` instead of `last`. When every call fails, the caller is told it succeeded and the failure goes unnoticed. This contradicts the doc comment ('returns the last error when every call failed'). Fix: `return last`. Also skip `time.Sleep(pause)` after the final attempt, which currently adds a pointless wait before returning.

findings.title: Shell command built by string concatenation: injection, and breaks on quotes or spaces
findings.detail: `pattern`, `stockFile` and `report` are pasted unescaped into an `sh -c` string. A pattern containing `'` (for example an item name like O'Brien) breaks the command or runs arbitrary shell commands, and file paths with spaces or shell metacharacters break the command or redirect output to the wrong place. Also, grep exits with status 1 when nothing matches, so a valid empty export comes back as an error. Fix: drop the shell. Use `exec.Command("grep", "-e", pattern, "--", stockFile)`, set `cmd.Stdout` to a file created with `os.Create(report)`, and treat exit code 1 as no matches. Better still, filter the lines in Go.

findings.title: Last, partial page is dropped (returns nil)
findings.detail: When `end > len(items)`, the function returns nil instead of the remaining items. With 25 items and a page size of 10, page 2 (items 20–24) comes back empty, so data silently disappears from the paginated view. Fix: if `start >= len(items)` return nil; otherwise set `end = min(end, len(items))` and return `items[start:end]`. Also guard against `number*size` overflowing.

findings.title: Every valid order line panics
findings.detail: The note loop at lines 24–25 accesses fields[len(fields)]. Every line with at least two fields panics, including valid lines both with and without a note. Remove the loop because the returned Line does not store the note.

findings.title: Invalid quantities are accepted silently
findings.detail: The parser discards the error from strconv.Atoi. Once the panic is fixed, a typo such as `widget;two` becomes a zero-quantity line that ReserveLines silently skips. An out-of-range integer can also be accepted as a different quantity. Return the conversion error with the line context.

findings.title: Order reservations bypass stock validation
findings.detail: The direct update to Reserved bypasses the stock's capacity and positive-count checks. An order can report success after overbooking stock, and a negative quantity can undo someone else's reservation. Apply the existing Stock.Reserve rules to each line and propagate validation errors.

findings.title: Concurrent reservations can lose updates
findings.detail: The write to Reserved runs outside the mutex used by Stock.Reserve and Stock.Free. Concurrent reservations against the same stock can lose updates while both callers receive success. Use the stock's existing mutex for validation and updates, as Stock.Reserve does.

findings.title: A failed order can leave stock partially reserved
findings.detail: If a later line names an unknown item, earlier lines have already updated stock. The caller gets an error without a record of those updates, so correcting the item and retrying can reserve the earlier lines twice. Resolve all items and validate the combined quantities under the stock locks before applying any updates.

findings.title: Order imports leave file descriptors open
findings.detail: LoadOrder never closes the file after opening it, including on early error returns. Repeated imports can accumulate open descriptors until garbage collection runs. Defer file.Close immediately after a successful open.

findings.title: Parsing any valid order line panics
findings.detail: The loop runs while index is less than or equal to len(fields), so every input with at least two fields eventually indexes past the slice. Both `widget;2` and `widget;2;note` panic. LoadOrder therefore panics on the first valid order line.

findings.title: Invalid quantities are silently converted into order lines
findings.detail: Once the loop bound is fixed, discarding the error from strconv.Atoi will let malformed quantities through as zero and out-of-range quantities through as the minimum or maximum int. The caller receives a successful parse with a quantity that differs from the input.

findings.title: An order line can omit its item
findings.detail: Once the loop bound is fixed, a line such as `;2` will parse successfully with an empty item key. This lets a malformed order reach reservation, where it can fail as an unknown item or match an empty key in the stock map.

findings.title: Loading orders leaks open file descriptors
findings.detail: LoadOrder opens the file without closing it on any path after a successful open. Repeated calls can exhaust file descriptors and cause subsequent file operations to fail.

findings.title: Long order lines fail at the scanner’s default limit
findings.detail: The default bufio.Scanner token limit is roughly 64 KiB. A line with a valid item and quantity and a long optional note can exceed that limit, causing LoadOrder to return a scanner error for input allowed by the documented format.

findings.title: Batch reservations can exceed stock capacity
findings.detail: ReserveLines increments Reserved without checking available units. For example, reserving 4 units against stock with 3 free succeeds and makes Free return a negative count. A sufficiently large increment can also wrap Reserved.

findings.title: Batch reservations accept nonpositive quantities
findings.detail: Stock.Reserve rejects counts of zero or less. ReserveLines silently skips zero and applies negative quantities directly, allowing an order to undo existing reservations or drive Reserved below zero.

findings.title: Batch reservations bypass the stock mutex
findings.detail: ReserveLines writes Reserved without acquiring the mutex used by Stock.Reserve and Stock.Free. Concurrent calls on the same Stock race, and concurrent reservations can lose updates.

findings.title: An unknown item leaves earlier lines reserved
findings.detail: When a later item is missing from the map, ReserveLines returns an error after committing previous lines. A caller that corrects the missing item and retries the order reserves the earlier lines twice.

findings.title: A nil stock entry causes a panic
findings.detail: The map lookup succeeds when a key exists with a nil *Stock value. For a nonzero quantity, ReserveLines dereferences that pointer and panics instead of returning an error.

findings.title: Note loop indexes past end of fields, panicking on every line
findings.detail: The loop `for index := 2; index <= len(fields); index++ { note += fields[index] }` reads fields[len(fields)] on its last step. For the minimal valid input "item;3", len(fields)==2, so it reads fields[2] and panics with index out of range. The same happens for every input that passes the len<2 check. LoadOrder therefore panics on any non-empty order file. Smallest fix: use `index < len(fields)`, or remove the unused note loop, since note is thrown away with `_ = note`.

findings.title: ReserveLines bypasses locking and capacity check, allowing overbooking and data races
findings.detail: ReserveLines does `stock.Reserved += line.Quantity` directly. It does not take stock.mutex and does not check against Capacity, unlike Reserve. An order can reserve more than Capacity without any error, so Free() goes negative and the overbooking goes unnoticed. The write also races with concurrent Reserve and Free calls. Negative quantities are also accepted, and they reduce Reserved. Smallest fix: call `stock.Reserve(line.Quantity)` for each line and return its error. Reserve already locks, checks capacity and rejects count<=0.

findings.title: Partial reservation left in place when a later line fails
findings.detail: When a line names an unknown item, ReserveLines returns an error, but the earlier lines stay reserved. The same will happen for insufficient stock once F2 is fixed. The caller sees a failed order, but stock has been consumed for part of it, with no rollback. Smallest fix: check every line first (item exists, quantity is positive and fits) before changing anything. Alternatively, keep track of what was applied and undo it on error.

findings.title: Quantity parse errors are silently ignored and become 0
findings.detail: `quantity, _ := strconv.Atoi(...)` throws away the error. A malformed quantity such as "widget;abc" or "widget;3x" becomes 0. ReserveLines then skips 0-quantity lines without saying anything, so a corrupted order line disappears without any error. Smallest fix: return an error when Atoi fails, and reject quantities <= 0 in ParseLine.

findings.title: Opened file is never closed
findings.detail: LoadOrder calls os.Open but never closes the file, on the success path or the error path. Each call leaks a file descriptor. Smallest fix: add `defer file.Close()` right after the error check.

findings.title: ParseLine indexes past the end of fields and panics on every line
findings.detail: The note loop runs `for index := 2; index <= len(fields); index++` and reads fields[index]. When index reaches len(fields), the read is out of range. A well-formed "item;3" has len 2, so fields[2] panics at once. Every line that gets past the length check panics, so LoadOrder crashes on any non-empty order file. The bound should be `<`.

findings.title: ReserveLines modifies Reserved without holding the stock mutex
findings.detail: `stock.Reserved += line.Quantity` runs without stock.mutex. Reserve and Free take that lock, so ReserveLines running alongside them, or alongside another ReserveLines call, is a data race. It can lose updates and corrupt the reserved count. It should call stock.Reserve(line.Quantity) or take the lock.

findings.title: ReserveLines skips the capacity and positive-quantity checks
findings.detail: It adds the quantity straight to Reserved and never checks it against Capacity, so an order can reserve more than exists. Free() then goes negative. A negative quantity is also accepted and lowers Reserved, which releases stock that other orders hold. Reserve exists to stop both of these, and ReserveLines does not use it.

findings.title: Bad quantity is silently parsed as 0 and the line is dropped
findings.detail: ParseLine discards the error from strconv.Atoi. A value like "abc", "2.5" or an empty quantity becomes 0 and no error is returned. ReserveLines then skips lines with quantity 0. A malformed order line is therefore lost without any report instead of being rejected.

findings.title: LoadOrder never closes the opened file
findings.detail: The file from os.Open is never closed: there is no defer file.Close(), and it stays open on the error return paths too. Each call leaks a file descriptor, and a long-running process will run out of descriptors.

findings.title: ReserveLines is not atomic: an error leaves earlier lines reserved
findings.detail: When an item is unknown partway through the order, the function returns an error, but the lines before it are already added to Reserved and nothing rolls them back. The caller sees the order as failed while stock is still held for it.

findings.title: Cache misses fresh entries and serves expired values
findings.detail: The expiration check is reversed. Get returns a miss while the entry is fresh and returns the cached value at or after expiration, so callers can silently use stale lookup results. Return a miss when `!found.expires.After(cache.Now())`.

findings.title: Concurrent cache reads and writes can terminate the process
findings.detail: Get reads `entries` without taking the mutex used by Put. Overlapping lookups and updates can trigger a fatal concurrent map read/write error and terminate the process. Guard the lookup with the same mutex.

findings.title: Invalid releases can let reservations exceed stock capacity
findings.detail: Release subtracts the count unconditionally. Retrying a release can drive Reserved below zero, causing Free to report more than Capacity and allowing later reservations beyond physical stock. A negative count also adds reserved units. Validate that the count is positive and no greater than Reserved under the lock, and return an error without changing stock when validation fails.

findings.title: Cache lookups reject fresh entries and return expired entries
findings.detail: Get returns a miss while the expiration time is in the future. At or after expiration, it returns the stored value as a hit, so callers miss fresh values and can reuse stale values indefinitely.

findings.title: Concurrent cache reads and writes can crash the process
findings.detail: Get reads the entries map without acquiring the mutex held by Put. Concurrent lookups and inserts race even on different keys and can terminate the process with a concurrent map read and map write error.

findings.title: Expired cache entries accumulate without bound
findings.detail: The cache retains every distinct key until the entire cache becomes unreachable. A long-lived cache that sees a steady stream of new keys can exhaust memory even when the TTL is short.

findings.title: Inserting into a zero-value Cache panics
findings.detail: A zero-value Cache has a nil clock and a nil entries map. Calling Put on a Cache embedded in a zero-initialized struct panics when it calls the nil clock.

findings.title: Invalid release counts corrupt stock accounting
findings.detail: Releasing more units than are reserved makes Reserved negative. Free then reports more units than Capacity, and subsequent reservations can accept more units than physically exist. A negative release count instead increases Reserved and can push it above Capacity.

findings.title: Releasing stock can race with batch reservations
findings.detail: Release holds the stock mutex, but ReserveLines updates the same Reserved field without it. Running the new release operation alongside a batch reservation for the same stock races and can lose either update, leaving an incorrect reserved total.

findings.title: Expiry check is inverted, so Get returns only expired values
findings.detail: `if found.expires.After(cache.Now()) { return 0, false }` treats an entry as a miss while it is still valid. After the TTL passes, the same entry is returned as a hit with `true`, and it is never removed. As a result, every cached lookup either misses or returns a stale value that callers accept as current, without any sign that something is wrong. Fix: return a miss when `!found.expires.After(cache.Now())`, that is, when `Now` is at or after `expires`. Optionally delete the expired entry at that point.

findings.title: Get reads the map without the mutex
findings.detail: Put locks `cache.mutex`, but Get reads `cache.entries` without locking it. When Get and Put run at the same time, Go's runtime can stop the program with "concurrent map read and map write", and the race detector reports it. Fix: call `cache.mutex.Lock(); defer cache.mutex.Unlock()` at the start of Get.

findings.title: Release does not check count, so Reserved can go negative
findings.detail: Release subtracts `count` with no checks. If a caller releases twice, or releases more than was reserved, `Reserved` drops below zero. A negative count does the opposite and adds to the reservation. When `Reserved` is negative, `Free()` reports more than `Capacity` and `Reserve` lets more units be sold than exist. Fix: return an error when `count <= 0 || count > stock.Reserved`, mirroring how `Reserve` checks its input.

findings.title: Expiry check inverted: live entries are misses, expired entries are hits
findings.detail: Get returns a miss when found.expires.After(now), meaning while the entry is still valid, and returns the value once it has expired. Every lookup within the TTL misses, and stale values are served forever after the TTL. The condition should be !found.expires.After(cache.Now()).

findings.title: Get reads the entries map without holding the mutex
findings.detail: Put writes cache.entries under cache.mutex but Get reads the map without locking. A concurrent Get and Put is a data race on a Go map, which can trigger the runtime's fatal 'concurrent map read and map write' error and crash the process.

findings.title: Release does not validate count, so Reserved can go negative
findings.detail: Release subtracts any count without checking that it is positive or no more than Reserved. Releasing too much, for example a double release, or passing a negative count drives Reserved below zero or above Capacity. Free() then reports more units than Capacity, or a negative number, and Reserve can oversell. Reserve rejects a count <= 0, but Release has no matching guard.

findings.title: Expired cache entries are never evicted
findings.detail: Nothing ever deletes an entry from the entries map: Get does not drop an expired entry and there is no sweep. With many distinct keys the map grows without bound, which leaks memory.

findings.title: Export interprets arguments as shell commands
findings.detail: The shell interprets all three Export arguments as command text. An ordinary filename with spaces or a search pattern with an apostrophe can break the export, and untrusted input can run commands with the caller's permissions. Invoke grep directly with the pattern and stock path as separate arguments, use `-e` and `--` to keep them from being parsed as options, and connect stdout to a file through Go.

findings.title: A failed export erases the previous report
findings.detail: Shell redirection truncates an existing report before grep opens the stock file or validates the pattern. A missing stock file or invalid pattern therefore destroys the previous report even though Export returns an error. Write to a temporary file beside the report and replace the report only after grep completes successfully.

findings.title: Retry reports success after every attempt fails
findings.detail: When every call to work fails, Retry saves the last error but returns nil after the loop. A caller can proceed as if a failed reservation or write succeeded. Return `last` after the loop.

findings.title: Pagination silently drops the final partial page
findings.detail: Page returns nil whenever the requested page extends past the end of the slice, even when its start is valid. For example, a caller paging through 11 items in groups of 10 silently misses the last item. Return nil when the start is out of range and cap the end at the slice length.

findings.title: Page arithmetic can overflow and panic
findings.detail: Large positive page numbers or sizes can overflow `number * size` or `start + size`. A negative result can pass the length check and panic during slicing. For nonempty input, reject `number > (len(items)-1)/size` before multiplying, then limit the page length to `len(items)-start` before adding.

findings.title: Retry waits after its last attempt
findings.detail: Retry sleeps after the final failed call even though there is no next attempt. A single failed attempt waits for the entire configured pause before returning. Sleep only when another attempt remains.

findings.title: Export interprets caller input as shell code
findings.detail: Export inserts the pattern and both file paths into shell source. If an untrusted caller controls any of these values, the shell can execute commands with the privileges of the calling process. Invoke grep directly with separate arguments and handle output through a file descriptor.

findings.title: Export misparses paths containing spaces
findings.detail: The paths are interpolated without argument boundaries. A stock path containing spaces can become multiple grep arguments, and a report path containing spaces can redirect output to the wrong file. Pass the stock path as one argument and open the report path directly.

findings.title: Export lets grep parse patterns and filenames as options
findings.detail: Grep can interpret a pattern or relative stock filename beginning with a hyphen as an option. A valid export can therefore fail or produce different output. Bind the pattern with -e and end option parsing before the filename.

findings.title: Export reports an error when no lines match
findings.detail: Grep exits with status 1 after a successful search that finds no matching lines. Export passes that status back as an error even though the empty report is the correct result.

findings.title: Export can erase an existing report or its own input
findings.detail: The shell truncates the report before grep opens the stock file or validates the pattern. A missing input file or invalid pattern can erase a previous report, and paths that refer to the same file cause the stock data itself to be erased before it is read. Write to a temporary file and replace the report only after a successful search.

findings.title: Page drops the final partially filled page
findings.detail: When the requested page starts within the slice but fewer than size items remain, Page returns nil and hides the remaining items. Cap the end at the slice length for an in-range start.

findings.title: Page can panic or return the wrong items after integer overflow
findings.detail: Both index calculations can overflow int. A wrapped end can pass the length check and lead to a slice-bounds panic, while a wrapped start can cause an out-of-range page number to return unrelated items. Check the page number against the item count before multiplying and bound the page length before adding.

findings.title: Retry reports success after every attempt fails
findings.detail: When all calls fail, the loop retains the last error but the function returns nil. Callers can proceed as though the work succeeded even though every attempt failed.

findings.title: Retry waits after its last attempt
findings.detail: Retry sleeps after the final failed call even though there is no next attempt. This adds the full pause to an exhausted retry, including when the caller requests only one attempt.

findings.title: Retry reports success when every attempt failed
findings.detail: After the loop the function runs `return nil`, but the doc comment says it returns the last error. When every call to `work` fails, the caller is told the work succeeded and the failure goes unnoticed. The same happens when attempts <= 0, because `work` never runs. Fix: return `last` after the loop. For attempts <= 0, return an error or call `work` at least once.

findings.title: Export can be used to run arbitrary shell commands
findings.detail: Export joins `pattern`, `stockFile` and `report` into one string and runs it with `sh -c`. A pattern that contains a single quote breaks the command by accident, for example an item name like `O'Brien`. A crafted pattern such as `x'; rm -rf ~; '` runs extra commands. File paths that contain spaces or shell metacharacters break the command too. Fix: drop the shell. Run `exec.Command("grep", "--", pattern, stockFile)`, set its Stdout to a file opened with os.Create(report), and treat grep's exit code 1 (no lines matched) as an empty report, not an error. Even better, filter the lines in Go.

findings.title: Page drops the last page when it is not full
findings.detail: When `end > len(items)`, the function returns nil instead of the remaining items. So with 25 items and a page size of 10, page 2 comes back empty and items 20–24 can never be reached. Fix: return nil only when `start >= len(items)`, and otherwise cap `end` at len(items). Large values of `number*size` can also overflow, so compare `number` with `len(items)/size` before multiplying.

findings.title: Retry waits again after the last failed attempt
findings.detail: `time.Sleep(pause)` also runs after the final attempt, so a call that has already failed waits one extra `pause` before it returns. Fix: sleep only when `attempt < attempts-1`.

findings.title: Shell command injection through pattern, stockFile and report
findings.detail: Export joins pattern, stockFile and report into a string and passes it to `sh -c`. A pattern that contains a single quote (for example `x'; rm -rf ~; echo '`) ends the quoting, so the shell runs whatever follows. File names with spaces or shell metacharacters are also run or split by the shell. Run grep directly with exec.Command("grep", "--", pattern, stockFile), and write its stdout to a file opened with os.Create(report).

findings.title: Retry returns nil when every attempt failed
findings.detail: When all attempts fail, the loop ends and the function returns nil, not `last`. Callers see success after a failed operation, which contradicts the doc comment. The function should return last.

findings.title: Last partial page is dropped
findings.detail: When end > len(items), Page returns nil. So a final page with fewer than size items is never returned: for 5 items with size 2, page 2 is empty when it should hold the 5th item, and with fewer than size items in total there are no pages at all. Return nil only when start >= len(items), and clamp end to len(items).

findings.title: Sleeps after the final failed attempt
findings.detail: time.Sleep(pause) also runs after the last attempt, so a call that has already failed waits one extra pause before it returns. Sleep only between attempts.

findings.title: No matches reported as an error; pattern treated as regex
findings.detail: grep exits with status 1 when no line matches, so command.Run returns an error for a valid empty export. Because the shell redirection runs first, the report file is still created or truncated. The pattern is also read as a regular expression, so item names that contain characters like . or [ match the wrong lines; grep -F would match them literally.
